Convolutions in Practice

Variants, segmentation and the vision pipeline around them

Chapter 2.4 built the convolutional layer and used it to name a digit. Real vision work asks for more: a label for every pixel, layers that grow their view without growing their weights, layers that upsample instead of shrink, cheaper arithmetic, cleaner inputs, and networks that draw rather than read. On the right, a 29,465-weight U-Net trained on 2,600 photos from the Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset decides, pixel by pixel, which part of a photo it has never seen is the animal. Move your pointer over the photo to read its confidence at that pixel and see how much of the image that one output can look at.

The prior
Convolution is a dense layer with most weights forced to zero and the rest forced equal
The output
Segmentation: a probability for every pixel, decoded back up to full size
The pipeline
Normalise, augment, compute fast, and run the same filters at any image size

The idea

Convolution as an infinitely strong prior

A prior over weights says which models we believe in before seeing data. A weak prior, like a broad Gaussian, lets the data move the weights almost anywhere. A strong one pins them down. Push a prior to the limit and it becomes a hard rule: some values are simply forbidden. Seen this way, a convolutional layer is an ordinary fully connected layer with an infinitely strong prior on its weight matrix. Every hidden unit must use the same weights as its neighbour, just shifted one place along, and every weight outside a small window must be exactly zero. Pooling adds a second infinitely strong belief: the layer’s output should not change when the input shifts a little.

A strong prior is a bet. When it is right, it saves you from needing huge amounts of data. When it is wrong, the model underfits, because no amount of data can buy back a forbidden weight. Below, a linear layer W maps 16 pixels (one stretch of a row of a real pet photo) to 16 outputs. The hidden truth is either a 3-tap edge detector applied everywhere, which fits the prior, or the same detector with a gain that grows from left to right, which breaks it. A penalty of strength λ pulls W towards the convolutional pattern. Move λ from 0 to ∞ with only a dozen training rows, then switch the task.

\[ \begin{aligned} \hat W_\lambda &= \arg\min_W \sum_{n} \Vert \mathbf y_n - W\mathbf x_n \Vert^2 \\ &\quad + \lambda R(W) \\ R(W) &= \sum_{|i-j|>1} W_{ij}^2 \\ &\quad + \sum_{|i-j|\le 1} \big(W_{ij} - W_{i+1,\,j+1}\big)^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: fit the 16 × 16 matrix W to the training pairs (xn, yn) by least squares, plus a penalty R. The first sum charges for every weight outside the 3-wide band; the second charges whenever a weight in the band differs from the one diagonally below it, that is, whenever neighbouring units disagree. This is a Gaussian prior centred on “local and shared”, with precision λ.
Say it“W-hat is the W that minimises the squared error plus lambda times R, where R charges for weights outside the band and for differences along each diagonal.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{\lambda\to\infty} \hat W_{ij} &= \begin{cases} k_{\,j-i} & |j-i| \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\ \Longrightarrow\quad \mathbf y &= \mathbf k * \mathbf x \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: with an infinite penalty only zero-cost matrices survive: a band of three diagonals, each constant. Row i is the same three numbers k−1, k0, k1 shifted to position i, which is exactly a convolution with a 3-tap kernel. 256 free numbers have become 3.
Say it“As lambda goes to infinity, W i j becomes k of j minus i inside the band and zero outside, so y is k convolved with x.”

Variants of the basic function

Shared, tiled, locally connected

The convolution in a deep-learning library is not quite the one in a signal-processing textbook. It runs many kernels at once, each reading every input channel, so its kernel is a 4-D array Ko,c,a,b (output channel, input channel, row offset, column offset). It may skip positions with a stride s, which is a convolution followed by downsampling, computed without wasting the skipped outputs. And it decides what happens at the border with zero padding: valid (no padding, so the map shrinks by k − 1 every layer), same (pad just enough to keep the size) or full (pad so every input is visited k times, which grows the map).

Two relatives loosen the prior. A locally connected layer (“unshared convolution”) keeps the small window but gives every position its own weights: useful when a feature only makes sense in one place, such as a mouth in the lower half of an aligned face. Tiled convolution sits in between: it cycles through t different kernels as it moves, so neighbours differ but positions t apart share. Both leave room for features that vary across space while still keeping each unit’s view local. Biases have the same choices: one per channel (usual), one per tile, or one per position. Switch between the five kinds of layer and change the padding and stride; the colours show which connections share a weight.

\[ \begin{aligned} Z_{o,y,x} &= \sum_{c,a,b} K_{o,c,a,b}\; V_{c,\; s y + a,\; s x + b} \\ m &= \Big\lfloor \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} \Big\rfloor + 1 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: output channel o at position (y, x) adds up kernel weight K times input value V over every input channel c and every offset (a, b) of the k × k window, whose corner sits at (s y, s x) of the padded input. An input of length n, padded by p on each side, gives m outputs. Valid: p = 0. Same (s = 1, odd k): p = (k − 1)/2. Full: p = k − 1.
Say it“Z o y x is the sum over c, a, b of K o c a b times V c at s y plus a, s x plus b; the output length is the floor of n plus 2p minus k, over s, plus one.”
\[ \begin{aligned} P^{yx}_{c,a,b} &= V_{c,\; sy+a,\; sx+b} \\ Z^{\text{local}}_{o,y,x} &= \sum_{c,a,b} W_{o,y,x,c,a,b}\, P^{yx}_{c,a,b} \\ Z^{\text{tiled}}_{o,y,x} &= \sum_{c,a,b} K^{(y \bmod t,\; x \bmod t)}_{o,c,a,b}\, P^{yx}_{c,a,b} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: Pyx is the input window that output (y, x) reads. A locally connected layer indexes its weights by output position too, so it stores m2 kernels instead of one. A tiled layer stores t2 kernels and picks one by the position modulo t: t = 1 is ordinary convolution, and t = m is a locally connected layer.
Say it“Local: a separate W for every output position. Tiled: kernel number y mod t, x mod t.”
outputs m
distinct weights
connections

Seeing further, and going back up

Dilated and transposed convolutions

A stack of 3 × 3 layers sees only 2 more pixels per layer. A dilated (or atrous) convolution spreads the same 9 taps apart, reading every d-th pixel. Stack dilations 1, 2, 4, 8 and the view doubles with every layer while the weight count stays put. WaveNet uses this along time, and segmentation networks use it to see whole objects without pooling away their resolution. The catch is gridding: with the same dilation repeated, the taps never land on some pixels at all. Click the photo to move the output pixel, and try the three schedules.

\[ \begin{aligned} Z_{y,x} &= \sum_{a,b} K_{a,b}\, V_{y + d a,\; x + d b} \\ r_L &= 1 + \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} (k-1)\, d_\ell \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the kernel offsets a, b are multiplied by the dilation d before reading the input, so a 3 × 3 kernel with d = 4 covers a 9 × 9 patch using 9 numbers. After L layers with dilations d1…dL, one output depends on an rL × rL square. The heat map counts the paths from each input pixel to the chosen output, which is the output’s sensitivity when every weight is 1.
Say it“Z y x is the sum over a, b of K a b times V at y plus d a, x plus d b; the receptive field after L layers is one plus the sum of k minus one times d-ell.”
receptive field
holes inside it
weights (one channel)

Training a convolutional layer needs three operations, not one: the convolution itself, its gradient with respect to the kernel, and its gradient with respect to the input, so that the error can flow to earlier layers. Write the convolution as a matrix C acting on the flattened input (the matrices of the previous section). Then the third operation is multiplication by C⊤. That same operation, used on purpose, is the transposed convolution: each input value stamps a scaled copy of the kernel onto the output, with stamps s pixels apart, so the map grows by a factor of s. Decoders in segmentation networks and image generators are built from it. When k is not a multiple of s the stamps overlap unevenly, and a flat input comes out with a checkerboard (Odena, Dumoulin & Olah, 2016). Change k and s and watch the overlap pattern.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf z = C\,\mathbf v \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf v} &= C^{\top} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf z} \\ m_{\text{out}} &= (m - 1)\,s - 2p + k \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a strided convolution is a matrix C from n inputs to m outputs; the backward pass multiplies the output gradient by C⊤, taking m numbers back to n. A transposed-convolution layer is exactly that map with learned weights. Fed m values with stride s, padding p and kernel k, it produces (m − 1)s − 2p + k outputs.
Say it“If z is C v, the gradient with respect to v is C transpose times the gradient with respect to z; the transposed layer outputs m minus one times s, minus 2p, plus k values.”
output size
most / fewest stamps inside

Structured outputs

A label for every pixel

A classifier squeezes an image into one label. Many tasks want a whole structured output instead: a tensor S where Si,y,x is the probability that pixel (y, x) belongs to class i. That is semantic segmentation, and here i is just “pet” or “not pet”. The obstacle is pooling: every 2 × 2 pool halves the map, so the deep, wise features are coarse. Three answers: never pool (expensive), predict a coarser grid of labels (blurry), or go back up. The U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer & Brox, 2015) goes back up with transposed convolutions and adds skip connections that hand each decoder stage the sharp, early feature maps of the same size.

Neighbouring pixels usually share a label, and a pixel-wise prediction ignores that. Pinheiro & Collobert (2014) fed a network its own previous output and refined it step by step; a classic alternative is a graphical model that rewards neighbours for agreeing. The “refine” slider applies the simplest such model, a mean-field update of an Ising prior, on top of the network’s probabilities. Compare the network with and without skips, then add a few refinement steps.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal L &= -\frac{1}{HW}\sum_{y,x} \ell_{yx} \\ \ell_{yx} &= t_{yx}\ln p_{yx} + (1-t_{yx})\ln(1-p_{yx}) \\ \text{IoU} &= \frac{|\,P \cap T\,|}{|\,P \cup T\,|} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: training scores every pixel with −ℓ, the cross-entropy between the true label t (1 = pet) and the predicted probability p, and averages over all H·W pixels. Testing thresholds p at τ to get the predicted set P and compares it with the true set T: intersection over union is 1 for a perfect outline and punishes both missed fur and invented pet.
Say it“The loss is minus the average over pixels of t log p plus one minus t log one minus p; IoU is the size of P and T over the size of P or T.”
\[ q^{(t+1)}_{yx} = \sigma\Big( z_{yx} + \beta \!\!\sum_{(y',x') \sim (y,x)}\!\! \big(2q^{(t)}_{y'x'} - 1\big) \Big) \]
Read it as: z is the network’s logit at a pixel and q its current belief. Each step nudges the logit by β for every one of the four neighbours that leans “pet” and against it for every one that leans “background”. The same small update, repeated: a recurrent refinement, here with one hand-set weight β instead of a learned network.
Say it“The new q is sigma of z plus beta times the sum over the four neighbours of two q minus one.”

Data types and efficient algorithms

Any shape of data, computed fast

Convolution needs only that the data sit on a grid whose axes mean “nearby”. One axis: an audio waveform (one channel) or a recording of a skeleton’s joint angles over time (one channel per angle). Two axes: a spectrogram (frequency by time), or a colour photo with three channels. Three axes: a CT scan, or a colour video. And because the same kernel is simply applied more or fewer times, one network can take images of different sizes: a network built only of convolutions, pooling and upsampling (fully convolutional) maps an n × n photo to an n × n mask for any n its pooling can divide. This only makes sense when the sizes differ in extent of the same kind of measurement (a bigger photo), not when they hold different kinds of things. Feed the same pet to the trained U-Net at five sizes.

best size for this pet (IoU)
multiply-adds at 96 vs 48

Convolution dominates the cost of a vision network, so it pays to compute it cleverly. The convolution theorem turns it into pointwise multiplication: Fourier-transform image and kernel, multiply, transform back, which wins for big kernels. A separable kernel, one that is an outer product of a column and a row, can be applied as a 1-D pass down the columns and another along the rows: 2k multiplications per pixel instead of k2. Most kernels are not exactly separable, but the singular value decomposition writes any kernel as a sum of separable pieces, and a few often suffice. (Winograd’s minimal filtering, used in cuDNN for 3 × 3 kernels, is another trick in the same spirit.) Pick a kernel and lower the rank r: watch the cost and the error.

\[ \begin{aligned} K &= \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i\, \mathbf u_i \mathbf v_i^{\top} \\ K_r &= \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i\, \mathbf u_i \mathbf v_i^{\top} \\ \frac{\Vert K - K_r \Vert_F}{\Vert K \Vert_F} &= \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i>r}\sigma_i^2}{\sum_i \sigma_i^2}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the SVD writes the k × k kernel as k separable pieces (column ui times row vi), weighted by singular values σi in decreasing order. Keeping r pieces gives the best rank-r kernel, and its relative error depends only on the singular values left out.
Say it“K is the sum of sigma i u i v i transpose; keep r terms, and the relative error is the root of the dropped sigma-squares over all sigma-squares.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \text{direct:}\;& N^2 k^2 \qquad \text{rank } r\text{:}\; 2\,r\,N^2 k \\ \text{FFT:}\;& \approx 3 \cdot 2N^2\log_2 N + 4N^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: multiply-adds to filter an N × N image with a k × k kernel. Direct convolution pays k2 per pixel; each separable piece pays k down the column and k along the row. The FFT route costs about three 2-D transforms (image, kernel, inverse) plus a complex product per frequency, whatever k is, so it only wins for large kernels.
Say it“Direct costs N squared k squared; rank r costs two r N squared k; the FFT costs about six N squared log N.”
kernel error ‖K − Kr‖ / ‖K‖
multiply-adds per pixel
output error (RMS / RMS)

Features without back-propagation

Random, hand-made and unsupervised filters

Learning convolution kernels is the expensive part of training: every gradient step runs the whole network forwards and backwards. There are three cheaper ways to get kernels. Random: draw them and never change them. Hand-designed: write down edge or Gabor detectors. Unsupervised: cluster image patches with k-means and use the cluster centres as kernels (Coates, Lee & Ng, 2011). Then train only the last layer, a convex problem. Jarrett et al. (2009) found that random filters followed by rectification and pooling worked surprisingly well, and Saxe et al. (2011) showed why: a conv-plus-pooling stage is selective for frequency and tolerant of shifts even with random weights. They suggested choosing architectures by testing them with random weights, at a fraction of the cost. Before 2012 many networks were also pre-trained layer by layer without labels; today end-to-end supervised training is the norm, and these ideas survive mainly where labels or compute are scarce.

Here each bank of 5 × 5 colour filters feeds a per-pixel logistic regression, fitted on 32 test pets and scored on 32 others. Nothing but the readout is trained. Compare the four banks, then draw a few new random banks.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf a_{yx} &= \text{relu}(\pm \mathbf r_{yx}) \\ \boldsymbol\phi_{yx} &= \big[\,\mathbf a,\; \bar{\mathbf a}^{7},\; \bar{\mathbf a}^{19},\; \mathbf v,\; \bar{\mathbf v}^{19}\big]_{yx} \\ p_{yx} &= \sigma\big(\mathbf w^{\top} \boldsymbol\phi_{yx} + b\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: ryx holds the F filters’ responses at the pixel, and a their positive and negative halves, rectified (2F numbers). These are kept as they are and averaged over 7 × 7 and 19 × 19 windows (the bars), a cheap stand-in for pooling and depth. The pixel’s colour v and its 19 × 19 average are added. Only w and b are learned, by L2-regularised logistic regression (C = 1).
Say it“a is the rectified responses; phi is a, its local averages, and the colour; p is sigma of w dot phi plus b.”
\[ \min_{\boldsymbol\mu_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_F} \sum_{n} \min_f \big\Vert \mathbf x_n - \boldsymbol\mu_f \big\Vert^2 \]
Read it as: xn are 4,000 random 5 × 5 × 3 patches from the fitting photos, each shifted to zero mean and scaled to unit length. k-means places F centres to minimise the squared distance from every patch to its nearest centre. The centres are typical patches, and become the kernels. No label is used.
Say it“Choose F centres to minimise the sum over patches of the squared distance to the nearest centre.”

Neuroscience and history

What the visual cortex suggested

Convolutional networks are the clearest success of brain-inspired AI. In the late 1950s and 1960s Hubel and Wiesel recorded single neurons in the cat’s primary visual cortex, V1, and found three properties that a convolutional layer copies. V1 is laid out as a map of the retina, so nearby neurons look at nearby places. Its simple cells respond to a roughly linear function of the light in a small patch: they act like detector units with a local kernel. Its complex cells respond to the same features but tolerate small shifts, and even the light/dark phase of an edge: that is pooling. Deeper areas repeat the pattern, until neurons in inferotemporal cortex fire for whole objects or faces whatever their position.

Measured simple-cell kernels are well described by Gabor functions: a stripe pattern under a Gaussian window. A complex cell can be modelled by squaring and adding two simple cells whose stripes are a quarter-cycle apart, a quadrature pair; the sum barely changes as an edge slides across. The brain also differs from a CNN: it moves its high-resolution fovea in saccades rather than seeing everything at once, it fuses other senses, it feeds information back down from higher areas, and its neurons are far richer than ReLUs. Shape the Gabor kernel, then compare the simple and complex cell on a drifting grating.

\[ \begin{aligned} w(x,y) &= \alpha\, e^{-\beta_x x'^2 - \beta_y y'^2} \cos(f x' + \phi) \\ x' &= x\cos\tau + y\sin\tau \\ y' &= -x\sin\tau + y\cos\tau \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: (x, y) is an offset from the centre of the cell’s patch, rotated by the preferred orientation τ into (x′, y′). The cosine makes stripes across x′ with frequency f and phase φ; the Gaussian, with widths set by βx and βy, keeps it local. The cell’s response to an image is the sum of w times the image, like one unit of a convolutional layer.
Say it“w is alpha times e to the minus beta-x x-prime squared minus beta-y y-prime squared, times cos of f x-prime plus phi.”
\[ \begin{aligned} s_\phi(I) &= \sum_{x,y} w_\phi(x,y)\, I(x,y) \\ c(I) &= \sqrt{\, s_{\phi}(I)^2 + s_{\phi+\pi/2}(I)^2 \,} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: sφ is a simple cell with phase φ, and its partner sφ+π/2 has its stripes shifted a quarter-cycle. A grating that drifts by d pixels shifts the phase of both responses by f·d, so each simple cell rises and falls, but the pair traces a circle and its radius c stays almost fixed. Squaring and summing is an L2 pool over phase, the complex cell’s invariance.
Say it“A simple cell sums w-phi times the image; the complex response is the square root of s-phi squared plus s-phi-plus-pi-over-two squared.”
simple cell: max / min over the drift
complex cell: max / min

A short history. Fukushima’s neocognitron (1980) already stacked simple-cell and complex-cell layers, but set its weights with a local, unsupervised rule. Time-delay neural networks shared weights across time for speech (Lang & Hinton, 1988; Waibel et al., 1989). LeCun and colleagues (1989) trained a 2-D convolutional network end to end with back-propagation to read handwritten zip codes, and by the late 1990s their networks were reading a sizeable share of the cheques written in the United States. Convolutional networks were among the first deep networks to train well with back-propagation, at a time when deep fully connected networks were thought too hard; the prior made them data-efficient and the shared weights made them cheap. In 2012 a GPU-trained convolutional network (Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton) won the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin, and modern deep learning took off from there.

The vision pipeline

Preprocessing, contrast normalisation and augmentation

Vision needs less preprocessing than most fields, but some is essential. Pixels must be on one scale, [0, 1] or [−1, 1], never 0–255 for some images and 0–1 for others. Many architectures need one fixed size, so images are cropped or resized; a fully convolutional net like ours does not strictly need it. Everything else either removes variation the model should not have to learn, or adds variation it should learn to ignore.

The biggest nuisance in photos is contrast: the same cat in dim and bright light. Global contrast normalisation subtracts each image’s mean and divides by its standard deviation, so any change of brightness or contrast of the form a·x + b (a > 0) vanishes exactly. Geometrically it puts every image on a sphere of radius s around the origin (in the space of mean-zero images). The U-Net on this page sees every photo through GCN with s = 1, λ = 0, ε = 0.01. Local contrast normalisation does the same in every small neighbourhood, so a shadowed half and a sunlit half both keep their detail. Change the lighting and the normalisation: the network’s answer cannot change under GCN until pixels start to clip.

\[ \begin{aligned} X'_{i,j,k} &= s\,\frac{X_{i,j,k} - \bar X}{\max(\epsilon,\, \sqrt{\lambda + v}\,)} \\ v &= \tfrac{1}{3rc}\textstyle\sum_{i,j,k}\big(X_{i,j,k}-\bar X\big)^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: X is an r × c × 3 image, X̄ its mean over all pixels and channels, and v the mean squared deviation from it. Subtract the mean, divide by the root-mean-square deviation √v, scale by s. λ softens the division and ε stops a blank image from being blown up by dividing by almost nothing.
Say it“X-prime is s times X minus its mean, over the larger of epsilon and the root of lambda plus the mean squared deviation.”
\[ \begin{aligned} X'_{i,j} &= \frac{X_{i,j} - \mu_{i,j}}{\max(\epsilon,\, \sigma_{i,j})} \\ \mu_{i,j} &= \sum_{a,b} g_{a,b}\, X_{i+a,\,j+b} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: local contrast normalisation. μi,j is a Gaussian-weighted mean (weights g summing to 1) of the neighbourhood of pixel (i, j), and σi,j the matching weighted standard deviation. Each pixel is compared only with its surroundings, which is close to what the retina does.
Say it“X-prime is X minus the local mean, over the larger of epsilon and the local standard deviation.”
pixels clipped
largest change in p(pet)
IoU, this pet

Dataset augmentation goes the other way: rather than remove variation, it manufactures it, training on transformed copies whose label is known not to change. For a segmentation network the label must be transformed with the image: flip the photo and you flip the mask. Our U-Net saw a random half of its training photos mirrored left to right, and nothing else. Its convolutions make it equivariant to shifts by design (up to the borders and the pooling grid); rotations and colour casts it was never shown. Pick a transformation and test the network on all 64 pets: each point is the mean IoU, measured against the transformed true masks.

mean IoU at this strength
untouched pets

Running the network backwards

Convolutional generative networks

A recognition network funnels a big image into a few numbers. A generator runs the other way: from a short code z to a full image, growing the map at every layer. Its layers are the transposed convolutions of the dilate section, sometimes called “deconvolutions”. Pooling has no exact inverse, since it throws information away, so Dosovitskiy et al. (2015) used un-pooling: copy each value into the corner of a 2 × 2 block, fill the rest with zeros, and let the next convolution smear it into place. GANs and VAEs (chapters 2.7 and 2.8) learn generators like this, and the shared kernels give their images local coherence for free.

The generator below turns 8 numbers into a 32 × 32 pet silhouette through a dense layer and three 4 × 4, stride-2 transposed convolutions (4 → 8 → 16 → 32). It was trained on the 3,200 trimaps with a simple, honest shortcut: each mask’s code is fixed to its first 8 principal-component scores, scaled to unit variance, so only the decoder is learned. Decoding each training mask’s own code reproduces it with an IoU of 0.844, against 0.808 for the linear PCA reconstruction from the same 8 numbers. Drawing z from a standard Gaussian therefore gives plausible but not guaranteed silhouettes; a VAE or GAN would learn the code too. Move the sliders, sample, or slide between two real pets.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf h_0 &= \text{relu}(W_0\,\mathbf z + \mathbf b_0) \in \mathbb R^{4\times4\times32} \\ \mathbf h_\ell &= \text{relu}\big(K_\ell \circledast^{\!\top}_{2} \mathbf h_{\ell-1} + \mathbf b_\ell\big), \quad \ell = 1, 2 \\ \hat{\mathbf x} &= \sigma\big(K_3 \circledast^{\!\top}_{2} \mathbf h_2 + b_3\big) \in [0,1]^{32\times32} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a dense layer maps the code to a 4 × 4 map with 32 channels. Each ⊛⊤2 is a transposed convolution with 4 × 4 kernels, stride 2 and padding 1, which doubles height and width: (m − 1)·2 − 2 + 4 = 2m. The last one has a single channel, squashed by σ into p(pet) per pixel. Training minimised pixel-wise cross-entropy against the true masks.
Say it“h-nought is relu of W z plus b; each h-ell is relu of a stride-two transposed convolution of the previous h; x-hat is sigma of the last one.”
\[ \text{unpool}(\mathbf h)_{2y+a,\;2x+b} = \begin{cases} h_{y,x} & a = b = 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]
Read it as: un-pooling doubles the map by placing each value at the top-left of its 2 × 2 block and zeros elsewhere. Un-pooling followed by an ordinary convolution computes exactly a stride-2 transposed convolution (its “insert zeros, then convolve” form), which is why modern generators use the latter directly.
Say it“Un-pooling puts h y x at position 2y, 2x and zeros in the other three places of the block.”
pixels with p ≥ 0.5
IoU with the real mask

Real-world project

Project: segmenting pets with a U-Net

The Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset (Parkhi, Vedaldi, Zisserman & Jawahar, 2012) has 7,349 photos of 37 breeds of cats and dogs, each with a hand-drawn trimap: pet, background, or an unsure band along the outline. Its official split has 3,680 “trainval” and 3,669 test photos. This chapter used a seeded random 2,600 of the trainval photos for training and 600 test photos for testing; 64 of those 600 are embedded in this page. Each photo was decoded, squashed to a square and averaged down to 48 × 48 pixels; each trimap was averaged over the same blocks, and a pixel counts as “pet” when at least half of its block is pet or outline. The dataset is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (copyright in the photos stays with their owners); the downsampled extract embedded in this page is shared under the same licence. Photos came from the dataset’s Hugging Face mirror (timm/oxford-iiit-pet), the trimaps from the original release.

The network is a U-Net shrunk to fit a web page: two 3 × 3 convolutions per stage, 8, 16 and 32 channels, two max-pools, two 2 × 2 transposed convolutions and a 1 × 1 output layer, 29,465 weights in all. It was trained in plain numpy (hand-written forward and backward passes, checked against finite differences to a relative error below 3 × 10−6) with Adam, batches of 8, a cosine learning-rate schedule from 0.002 and random left–right flips, for 3 epochs. A twin without skip connections (26,585 weights) was trained the same way. Both are stored in the page as 16-bit floats and run here, in your browser.

3 · How the training went

The reference in Python

import json, numpy as np
Z = np.load("pets48.npz"); ntr = int(Z["ntr"])                 # 2,600 trainval + 600 test pets, 48 x 48 RGB
X = Z["X"].astype(np.float64) / 255                              # uint8 -> [0, 1]
m = X.mean(axis=(1, 2, 3), keepdims=True)
X = (X - m) / np.maximum(1e-2, np.sqrt(((X - m) ** 2).mean(axis=(1, 2, 3), keepdims=True)))   # global contrast norm.
Y = Z["F48"] >= 0.5                                              # pet if >= half the cell is pet or border in the trimap
test = np.arange(ntr, len(X)); emb = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(64).choice(600, 64, replace=False)) + ntr

def conv(x, W, b):                                               # 3x3, stride 1, zero padding 1, then ReLU
    N, H, Wd, C = x.shape; xp = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (1, 1), (1, 1), (0, 0)))
    cols = np.concatenate([xp[:, a:a + H, c:c + Wd] for a in range(3) for c in range(3)], -1)
    return np.maximum(cols @ W.reshape(9 * C, -1) + b, 0)
def up(x, W, b):                                                 # transposed convolution, 2x2 kernel, stride 2
    N, H, Wd, C = x.shape; O = W.shape[-1]
    z = (x.reshape(-1, C) @ W.reshape(C, 4 * O)).reshape(N, H, Wd, 2, 2, O)
    return z.transpose(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).reshape(N, 2 * H, 2 * Wd, O) + b
pool = lambda x: x.reshape(x.shape[0], x.shape[1] // 2, 2, x.shape[2] // 2, 2, x.shape[3]).max(axis=(2, 4))
def unet(P, x, skip=True):
    c = lambda n, h: conv(h, P[n + ".W"], P[n + ".b"])
    e1 = c("e1b", c("e1a", x)); e2 = c("e2b", c("e2a", pool(e1))); bt = c("btb", c("bta", pool(e2)))
    u1 = up(bt, P["u1.W"], P["u1.b"]); d1 = c("d1b", c("d1a", np.concatenate([u1, e2], -1) if skip else u1))
    u2 = up(d1, P["u2.W"], P["u2.b"]); d2 = c("d2b", c("d2a", np.concatenate([u2, e1], -1) if skip else u2))
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(d2 @ P["hd.W"] + P["hd.b"])[..., 0]))      # p(pet) for every pixel

def scores(p, y):
    pr = p >= 0.5; i, u = (pr & y).sum((1, 2)), (pr | y).sum((1, 2))
    return (pr == y).mean(), np.mean(i / np.maximum(u, 1)), i.sum() / u.sum()
ref = {}
for tag in ("skip", "noskip"):
    P = {k: v.astype(np.float16).astype(np.float64) for k, v in np.load(f"unet_{tag}.npz").items()}   # as shipped: 16-bit
    print(f"U-Net, {tag:6s} {sum(v.size for v in P.values()):,} weights")
    p = np.concatenate([unet(P, X[test[i:i + 100]], tag == "skip") for i in range(0, 600, 100)])
    print("  600 test pets: pixel accuracy %.4f  mean IoU %.4f  pooled IoU %.4f" % scores(p, Y[test]))
    pe = unet(P, X[emb], tag == "skip"); ref[tag] = pe
    print("   64 embedded:  pixel accuracy %.4f  mean IoU %.4f  pooled IoU %.4f" % scores(pe, Y[emb]))
    print("   mean p(pet) of first three embedded pets:", np.round(pe[:3].mean((1, 2)), 10))
    pf = unet(P, X[emb][:, :, ::-1], tag == "skip")[:, :, ::-1]
    print("   flip, predict, flip back: mean |change in p| = %.4f" % np.abs(pf - pe).mean())
x0 = Z["X"][emb[:1]].astype(np.float64) / 255; x1 = 0.6 * x0 + 0.2            # dim the lighting, lift the black level
g = lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / max(1e-2, x.std())
print("GCN(0.6 x + 0.2) == GCN(x):", np.allclose(g(x0), g(x1)), " max diff %.1e" % np.abs(g(x0) - g(x1)).max())
np.savez("x057-ref.npz", **ref)

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A convolution is a dense layer under an infinitely strong prior: local windows, shared weights. The bet pays off when the task looks the same everywhere and causes underfitting when it does not; tiled and locally connected layers relax it.
  • Padding (valid, same, full), stride and dilation set the output size and the view: m = ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1, and stacked dilations grow the receptive field exponentially for free, at the risk of holes.
  • The gradient of a convolution with respect to its input is a transposed convolution, the same operation decoders and generators use to upsample; uneven overlap of its stamps makes checkerboards.
  • Structured outputs such as segmentation need a map back up to full size: a U-Net decodes with transposed convolutions and skip connections, is trained with per-pixel cross-entropy and judged by IoU; neighbour-agreement priors can refine it.
  • Around the network: normalise contrast (GCN, LCN), augment with label-preserving transformations, compute with separable or FFT tricks, and remember that random or unsupervised filters with a trained readout are a cheap, surprisingly strong baseline.

Check your understanding

A 64 × 64 input passes a 5 × 5 convolution with stride 2. What size is the output with valid, and with same-style padding p = 2?

Valid: ⌊(64 − 5)/2⌋ + 1 = 29 + 1 = 30. With p = 2: ⌊(64 + 4 − 5)/2⌋ + 1 = 31 + 1 = 32, half the input, which is what “same” padding with stride 2 is meant to give.

Why might a face-verification network use a locally connected layer instead of a convolution near its top?

On aligned faces each region has a fixed meaning (eyes at the top, mouth at the bottom), so the translation-sharing prior is wrong there: a mouth detector is useless in the eye region. Unshared weights let each position learn its own features, at the cost of many more parameters.

Three layers of 3 × 3 convolutions with dilations 1, 2 and 4: how large is the receptive field, and how many weights per channel pair?

r = 1 + 2·(1 + 2 + 4) = 15, so 15 × 15, with 3 × 9 = 27 weights. Three undilated layers would see only 7 × 7 with the same 27 weights.

A U-Net without skip connections gets the rough location of the pet right but blurs the outline. Why?

Its only path to the output runs through the 12 × 12 bottleneck, so fine spatial detail has to be squeezed into coarse feature maps and regenerated by the decoder. Skip connections hand the decoder the full-resolution early maps, where edges are still sharp.

Why does global contrast normalisation make a network exactly blind to the change x → 0.6x + 0.2, but not to a strong red colour cast?

GCN subtracts one mean and divides by one standard deviation for the whole image, which exactly undoes one shared scale a > 0 and offset b (as long as nothing clips). A colour cast scales the three channels differently; after GCN the channels still differ, so the network sees a different input.
